questions.prompt: What is the quark composition of a proton?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a proton is two up quarks and one down quark (uud), giving charge $+\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = +1$.
questions.feedbackWrong: The proton's charge of +1 comes from two up quarks ($+\frac{2}{3}$ each) and one down quark ($-\frac{1}{3}$): uud.

mistakes.correction: udd is the neutron — its charges sum to zero, which cannot be the proton.

mistakes.misconception: Includes a strange quark, which is not part of ordinary nucleons.
mistakes.correction: Strange quarks appear in strange particles like kaons and hyperons, never in protons.

questions.prompt: Light of frequency $8.0 \times 10^{14}$ Hz strikes a metal surface with work function 2.3 eV. Enter the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons in eV, to 2 significant figures. (Use $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$ J s, $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J.)
In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light (frequency unchanged, above threshold) increases which quantity?
options: Number of photoelectrons emitted per second
The work function of the metal
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — greater intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons emitted per second. Each photon's energy is unchanged.
questions.feedbackWrong: Intensity is the number of photons per second. Photon energy depends only on frequency, so electron kinetic energies do not change — only their number does.

mistakes.misconception: Treats light as a wave whose energy scales with intensity.
mistakes.correction: The photon model is the whole point: one photon one electron, and $KE_{max} = hf - \phi$ contains no intensity term.

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of molecular motion, why the pressure of a fixed mass of gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
questions.guidance: Link temperature to kinetic energy, then kinetic energy to the force and frequency of molecular collisions with the walls.

markScheme.text: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy / speed of the molecules.
Molecules collide with the container walls more frequently.
Each collision transfers greater momentum / exerts greater force on the wall.
Pressure is force per unit area, so pressure increases.

questions.prompt: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium (specific heat capacity 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated by a 60 W heater for 5 minutes, with no heat losses. Enter the temperature rise in K, to 2 significant figures.
A fixed mass of ideal gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — Boyle's law: $pV$ is constant at fixed temperature, so halving V doubles p.
questions.feedbackWrong: At constant temperature $pV = \text{constant}$ (Boyle's law). Volume halved means pressure doubled.

mistakes.misconception: Assumes pressure is proportional to volume.
mistakes.correction: Pressure is INVERSELY proportional to volume — compressing the gas pushes molecules into less space, increasing wall collision rate.

questions.prompt: Compare alpha and beta-minus decay: state what changes in the nucleus in each case, and give one difference in their ionising or penetrating behaviour.

markScheme.text: Alpha: nucleus emits 2 protons and 2 neutrons — proton number falls by 2, nucleon number by 4.
Beta-minus: a neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino — proton number rises by 1, nucleon number unchanged.
Alpha is strongly ionising but weakly penetrating (stopped by paper/skin); beta is less ionising and more penetrating (stopped by a few mm of aluminium).

questions.prompt: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. To what Celsius temperature must it be heated at constant pressure for its volume to reach 450 cm³? Enter the answer in °C.

stepChecks.label: $V/T$ constant with T in kelvin: $T_1 = 300$ K

mistakes.misconception: Uses Celsius directly in the gas law ratio.
mistakes.correction: Gas law temperatures must be absolute — convert to kelvin first (27 °C = 300 K), then convert the answer back.
